textTitles: The town that grew its own doctors

texts.title: The town that grew its own doctors

paragraphs.text: Every country with a large countryside has the same complaint: doctors train in cities and stay there. The pattern is old, well documented and stubbornly resistant to the obvious remedies. Paying rural doctors more helps a little, and only while the money lasts; obliging newly qualified doctors to serve a few years outside the cities fills the posts and empties them again the moment the obligation ends. Over the past thirty years a handful of medical schools have tried something slower, and the results are interesting enough that health ministries now send people to look at them.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The idea is easy to state and hard to do. Instead of recruiting the students with the highest marks from wherever they happen to live, and then trying to persuade them to move, choose students who already come from country towns, teach a good part of the course in those towns rather than in a teaching hospital, and let the students spend long placements with the same rural practice rather than rotating through a city ward every six weeks. The bet is that a doctor who grew up in such a place, trained in such a place and has friends in such a place is more likely to work in one.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The evidence for the first part of the bet is the strongest. Across many studies and several countries, the single best predictor of where a doctor will practise is where they grew up: students from rural backgrounds are roughly two to three times more likely to end up in rural practice than classmates from cities, whatever else is done to them during training. Long rural placements add to this, and they also work for students from cities, though less powerfully. The two effects are largely independent, which is convenient for anyone designing a programme.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Doing it properly is expensive in ways that are easy to underestimate. A city teaching hospital has hundreds of patients and dozens of teachers in one building; a rural programme must pay a general practitioner to teach two students in a town of four thousand people, and must find somewhere for the students to live. Supervision is thinner, so the curriculum has to be written more carefully, and examiners have to travel. Several programmes that looked good on paper failed because the teaching load fell on doctors who were already the only ones in the district.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: There is also a question nobody likes to ask out loud: whether the training is as good. The honest answer, from the comparisons that exist, is that it is different rather than worse. Students in rural programmes see fewer rare diseases and more common ones, do more procedures themselves and earlier, and perform about the same in national examinations, with a small advantage in general practice and a small disadvantage in some hospital specialities. If the aim is to produce specialists for city hospitals, the model is the wrong one; if the aim is to produce doctors for small towns, that is exactly what it does.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The most successful schemes turn out to share features that have little to do with medicine. They recruit at school, years before applications open, so that a fifteen-year-old in a farming district can see the path. They keep a student in one community long enough to be recognised in the shop. They accept partners into the calculation, because a doctor with a partner who cannot find work locally will leave whatever their own preferences. And they invest in the practices that host students, since a doctor who is supported and paid to teach stays, while an unsupported one burns out and the training site closes with them.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: It is worth being careful with the numbers that programmes publish. Retention is usually reported as the share of graduates working rurally at some point after qualification, which counts a doctor who stayed eighteen months and one who has been there twenty years as the same thing. The figures that matter are longer: where is the cohort ten years later, and who is still in the same district? The programmes with the best long-term figures tend to be the oldest, which may mean that they are better, or simply that they have had time to learn from a generation of mistakes.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: None of this closes the gap. A country that trains a hundred rural-origin doctors a year and needs three hundred will still be short, and the shortage is worst where it is hardest to fix: remote districts with small populations and long distances. What the approach does is change the shape of the problem. Instead of persuading reluctant people to go somewhere they do not want to be, it finds people who would rather be there anyway, and removes the reasons they would otherwise have to leave. That is a slower answer than a bonus payment, and it is the only one that has been shown to last.
paragraphs.label: H
